questions.question: Which of the following best describes why extra information (such as tables or graphical models) is added to natural‑language requirements?

options.A: To replace the need for any textual description altogether.
options.B: To illustrate how computations, system‑state changes, and user interactions proceed.
options.C: To ensure that the requirements are written in a programming language.
options.D: To reduce the amount of documentation that must be reviewed.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] Adding tables or graphics helps show computation flow, state changes, user interaction, and action sequences, as explained on page 24.

---

questions.question: In the context of describing an insulin pump, what does the tabular specification primarily capture?

options.A: The hardware components of the pump.
options.B: The sequence of computational steps and resulting system states.
options.C: The user’s emotional response to insulin dosage.
options.D: The marketing strategy for the device.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The tabular specification is used to detail the computation in the insulin pump (page 24).

---

questions.question: How do use cases contribute to the Unified Modeling Language (UML)?

options.A: They provide a method for writing low‑level code directly in UML diagrams.
options.B: They serve as a graphical and textual way to describe user‑system interactions, a core UML feature.
options.C: They replace all other types of UML diagrams.
options.D: They focus exclusively on database schema design.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Use cases describe interactions using graphics and structured text and are now a fundamental UML feature (page 25).

---

questions.question: Which statement correctly reflects the historical origin of use cases?

options.A: They were first introduced in the Waterfall model.
options.B: They originated in the Objectory method before becoming part of UML.
options.C: They were created by the Agile Manifesto authors.
options.D: They were derived from formal mathematical specifications.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Use cases were introduced in the Objectory method (Jacobsen et al., 1993) and later incorporated into UML (page 25).

---

questions.question: At what point in the software development lifecycle do verification and validation (V&V) activities begin according to the text?

options.A: After the code has been fully implemented.
options.B: Only during the final acceptance testing phase.
options.C: As soon as requirements become available and continue throughout development.
options.D: When the maintenance team takes over the product.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] V&V start when requirements are available and persist through all stages (page 37).

---

questions.question: In Figure 8.2, what is the purpose of the arrows that connect software inspections and testing to various stages of the process?

options.A: To indicate that inspections replace testing at every stage.
options.B: To show the specific stages where each technique can be applied for V&V support.
options.C: To illustrate the flow of money between departments.
options.D: To map the timeline for releasing the software to the market.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The arrows indicate the stages where inspections and testing may be used to support V&V (page 38).

---

questions.question: Which benefit is most directly associated with using a tabular specification for an insulin pump’s computation?

options.A: It automatically generates the pump’s firmware.
options.B: It clarifies the step‑by‑step logic and state transitions for stakeholders.
options.C: It eliminates the need for any user documentation.
options.D: It provides a visual animation of insulin delivery.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Tabular specs make computation steps and state changes explicit, aiding understanding (page 24).

---

questions.question: When describing a scenario, the “normal flow of events” refers to:

options.A: The sequence of actions that occurs under typical, expected conditions.
options.B: The list of error messages the system might produce.
options.C: The alternative pathways that are never used.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The normal flow details the usual sequence of events in a scenario (page 19).

---

questions.question: How does combining a graphical model with structured text in a use case improve requirements communication?

options.A: It reduces the need for stakeholder meetings.
options.B: It allows both visual and detailed textual representation of interactions, catering to different stakeholder preferences.
options.C: It enforces a strict programming syntax.
options.D: It eliminates the need for any further validation activities.

questions.explanation: [Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Use cases use graphics plus structured text to describe interactions, enhancing clarity for varied audiences (page 25).
